sentences: Beneath an old tree, a mother dog sits with her puppies gathered close against her.
She bends her head to look down at the little one asleep in her embrace, while the others press in at her side.
It is a quiet moment, as if even the wind has paused.
This is Mother Dog and Puppies, often called Mogyeondo, painted by Yi Am in the early Joseon period.
It is painted on paper and mounted as a tall hanging scroll, 163 centimetres high and 55.
5 centimetres wide.
It belongs to the National Museum of Korea in Seoul.
Yi Am was born in 1499.
He was a great-grandson of Grand Prince Imyeong, the fourth son of King Sejong, and a member of the royal clan who held the title Duseongnyeong.
He was not a professional court painter, yet he was famous for his paintings of animals.
The court knew his skill well.
The official annals of King Injong record that the royal secretariat recommended Yi Am, together with the painter Yi Sang-jwa, to paint the portrait of King Jungjong.
Now look closely at the mother's fur.
Where one colour gives way to another, there is no hard line.
The ink soaks into the paper and spreads naturally, so the coat shades softly from one tone into the next.
Instead of drawing outlines, Yi Am shaped the bodies with washes of ink.
Look at the mother's neck.
She wears a red collar hung with a small bell, a sign that she was a cherished dog in a noble household.
As a member of the royal family, Yi Am is thought to have been able to observe the court's hounds and hawks at close range.
Now look at the puppies.
With their long, drooping ears and round little bodies, they resemble the native dogs of Korea.
One puppy sleeps in its mother's embrace, while the other two stay close beside her, their eyes turned toward each other.
The background is almost empty.
Only the trunk of the tree and a few branches are sketched in with simple strokes, so our eyes settle naturally on the family of dogs.
Below the tree, on the right, you can find the artist's seal.
Yi Am is said to have learned from the style of a Southern Song Chinese painter when he was young.
Yet his puppies have a plain, innocent charm that feels entirely Korean.
Scholars see this tender way of painting animals passed down to later Joseon artists such as Byeon Sang-byeok, who became famous for his cats.
His influence may even have crossed the sea.
One study points out that the puppies painted by the Japanese artist Tawaraya Sotatsu in the Edo period use the same soft pools of ink, and it explores whether they were inspired by Yi Am's dogs.
Step back and see the whole scroll.
Five hundred years ago, a royal painter chose to record not a great event but a quiet afternoon with a mother and her young.
Today, give the small lives around you one more tender look.
